sections.h2: What does the Franklin County Recorder of Deeds do?
sections.html:
The Recorder of Deeds keeps the public land record for Franklin County, Missouri. A deed that moves a house from one owner to another, and the deed of trust or release that goes with a loan, becomes part of that record once the office accepts it. The county seat is Union, and the county's home page carries a Record My Deeds link next to its tax payment and marriage license links.

Other county offices rely on what the Recorder files. The county assessor says it receives and processes more than 10,000 instruments and deeds a year from the county GIS department, and it uses them to keep ownership and parcel records current. Over 6,300 subdivisions are on file in the county. A deed that never gets recorded leaves the old owner's name on that trail.

Land titles in this county have a long paper trail. The Spanish built the log fort San Juan del Misuri at present-day Washington between 1796 and 1803, Daniel Boone settled the area from 1799, and the county was organized in 1818. Many parcels today trace back through nineteenth-century German farm families who arrived from 1833, so older deeds in a chain of title can carry spellings and descriptions that differ from today's plats.

Ask the office directly for its current room, hours and accepted payment types before you travel, and ask whether your title company can file for you.

sections.h2: Why does a recorded deed matter for a Franklin County sale?
sections.html:
Franklin County is a big, growing place for a Missouri county. The Census Bureau estimates 108,090 people in July 2025 across 922.65 square miles of land, about 113.5 people per square mile as of 2020. There are 43,036 households with 2.44 people each, and 90.1 percent of residents stayed in the same house over the prior year.

Homes here carry real costs. Median monthly owner costs are $1,442 with a mortgage and $505 without one, while median gross rent is $893. The county issued 794 building permits in 2025, so new houses are a steady part of the market.

A recorded deed is the proof of ownership for the next buyer's lender, and for the assessor's notices. Under RSMo 137.180 an assessor who raises a value must notify the record owner, so a buyer whose deed is not on file may see mail go to the former owner.

sections.h2: What format rules must a document meet before the Recorder accepts it?
sections.html:
RSMo 59.310 lets a Missouri recorder of deeds refuse a document that does not meet the page rules. A county can still record a nonconforming document for an extra $25. These are the state's main format rules:

  • Pages are printed on one side only and are not permanently bound or on a continuous form
  • Type is at least eight-point, in black or dark ink, and clear enough to copy
  • Paper is white or light colored, at least 20-pound weight, with no watermarks
  • Signatures are in dark ink with the name typed, printed or stamped beneath
  • The top margin is at least three inches on the first page, kept clear for the Recorder's certification, and every other margin is at least three-quarters of an inch

Documents signed before 2002, military separation papers, papers signed outside the United States, certified copies and court judgments are exempt from these format rules. A rejected paper comes back to the person who presented it with the reason it was refused.

sections.h2: What must the first page of a deed show?
sections.html:
Below the three-inch top margin on page one, state law asks for the items that identify the transaction. If they do not fit, the first page must say where in the document they appear.

  • The title of the document and its date
  • The names of all grantors with their marital status, and the names of all grantees
  • Any statutory addresses
  • The legal description of the property
  • Book and page references, where a statute calls for them

The legal description is the line most often copied wrongly. Copy it from the vesting deed or the title commitment, not from a tax bill, and have the title company read it before signing. A mistake there can mean a corrective deed and a second round of fees.

sections.h2: What are the Missouri recording fees at the Franklin County Recorder?
sections.html:
RSMo 59.310 sets the amounts a recorder may charge for services. The statute lists the following.

Statutory recorder fees under RSMo 59.310 (confirm total with the office)
ServiceFee
Recording a deed or instrument$5 first page, $3 each added page
Release or assignment of more than one item$5 per item beyond the first
Nonconforming documentExtra $25
Copy of a recorded instrumentUp to $2 first page, $1 each added page
Certificate and seal outside recording$1
Plat or survey of a subdivision$25 per sheet
Survey of one or more tracts$5 per sheet

These are the statute's base amounts. Under those base rates a five-page deed comes to $17. Ask the Franklin County office for the total on your page count before you mail a check.

sections.h2: Which taxes should be settled before a Franklin County deed is recorded?
sections.html:
Recording does not clear property tax. The Franklin County Collector, Doug Trentmann, is in Room 103 at 400 E Locust in Union and answers at 636-583-6353. The Collector bills for the county and 64 other taxing entities, so one parcel can owe to several of them on a single statement.

Taxes are due by December 31. After that they are delinquent, and the state adds an 18 percent penalty on the year's delinquency under RSMo 140.100. Delinquent land is offered for sale on the fourth Monday in August under RSMo 140.150, and the owner can pay what is owed up to the moment of the sale.

A purchaser who buys a house less than 30 days after the county mailed the tax statement may take an assessment appeal straight to the State Tax Commission, which says so in its guidance. In every other case the Board of Equalization comes first, and its filing date is the second Monday in July.

sections.h2: How do I record a deed after selling a Franklin County house?
sections.html:
Many sales close through a title company, which can prepare the deed, collect the fee and file it. For a private sale or a family transfer, have the deed drafted to the page rules above, check the legal description and then deliver it to the Recorder. Keep the recorded copy, since that is the proof the transfer went through.

Before closing, tell the title company which tax years are open and whether any lien, such as a judgment or a mechanic's claim, sits on the property. If the house was inherited or has tenants, ask the title company what has to be recorded first, and what a cash buyer will pay for at closing.

Give the buyer a clear contact for the Collector and the Assessor.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Franklin County, Missouri?
faqs.a: At the county Recorder of Deeds. The county website's home page has a Record My Deeds link. Contact the office for its room, hours and payment methods, or have your title company file for you.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Franklin County?
faqs.a: The statute's base fee is $5 for the first page and $3 for each later page. The office can quote the full total for your page count.

faqs.q: Why did the Recorder reject my deed?
faqs.a: Usually a format problem. RSMo 59.310 requires a three-inch top margin, dark ink, at least eight-point type and the first-page details. A rejected document is returned with a written reason, and a nonconforming one can be recorded for an extra $25.

faqs.q: Does recording a deed pay off property taxes?
faqs.a: No. Taxes are owed to the Franklin County Collector at 636-583-6353 and are due by December 31. Unpaid land can go to the fourth Monday in August sale.

faqs.q: Which Franklin County cities does the Recorder cover?
faqs.a: The whole county. That includes Union, Washington, Pacific, Sullivan, New Haven, St. Clair, Berger and Gerald, and unincorporated areas such as Gray Summit and Villa Ridge.
